{{Short description|On surjectivity of linear map to anti-dual}}
In mathematics, specifically in [[functional analysis]] and [[Hilbert space]] theory, the '''fundamental theorem of Hilbert spaces''' gives a necessary and sufficient condition for a [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]] [[pre-Hilbert space]] to be a Hilbert space in terms of the canonical isometry of a pre-Hilbert space into its [[anti-dual]]. 

== Preliminaries ==

=== Antilinear functionals and the anti-dual ===

Suppose that <math>H</math> is a [[topological vector space]] (TVS). 
A function <math>f:H\to\mathbb{C}</math> is called [[Semilinear map|semilinear]] or [[Antilinear map|antilinear]]{{sfn | Trèves | 2006 | pp=112–123}}  if for all <math>x,y\in H</math> and all scalars <math>c</math>,

*<math>f</math> is [[Additive map|additive]]: <math>f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)</math>;
*<math>f</math> is [[Antilinear map|conjugate homogeneous]]: <math>f(c\,x)=\bar{c}\,f(x)</math>.

The vector space of all continuous antilinear functions on <math>H</math> is called the [[anti-dual space]] or [[Complex conjugate vector space|complex conjugate dual space]] of <math>H</math> and is denoted by <math>\overline{H}^{\prime}</math>. (In contrast, the continuous dual space of <math>H</math> is denoted by <math>H^{\prime}</math>), which we make into a [[normed space]] by endowing it with the canonical norm (defined in the same way as the [[Operator norm|canonical norm]] on the [[continuous dual space]] of <math>H</math>.){{sfn | Trèves | 2006 | pp=112–123}}

=== Pre-Hilbert spaces and sesquilinear forms ===

A [[sesquilinear form]] is a map <math>B:H\times H\to\mathbb{C}</math> such that for all <math>y\in H</math>, the map defined by <math>x\mapsto B(x,y)</math> is [[linear map|linear]], and for all <math>x\in H</math>, the map defined by <math>y\mapsto B(x,y)</math> is [[Semilinear map|antilinear]].{{sfn | Trèves | 2006 | pp=112–123}}  
Note that in [[Physics]], the convention is that a sesquilinear form is linear in its ''second'' coordinate and antilinear in its first coordinate. 

A sesquilinear form <math>B</math> on <math>H</math> is called [[positive definite]] if <math>B(x,x)>0</math> for all non-0 <math>x\in H</math>; it is called non-negative if <math>B(x,x)\ge 0</math> for all <math>x\in H</math>.{{sfn | Trèves | 2006 | pp=112–123}}  
A sesquilinear form <math>B</math> on <math>H</math> is called a [[Hermitian form]] if in addition it has the property that <math>B(x, y) = \overline{B(y, x)}</math> for all <math>x,y\in H</math>.{{sfn | Trèves | 2006 | pp=112–123}}

=== Pre-Hilbert and Hilbert spaces ===

A [[pre-Hilbert space]] is a pair consisting of a vector space <math>H</math> and a non-negative sesquilinear form <math>B</math> on <math>H</math>; 
if in addition this sesquilinear form <math>B</math> is positive definite then <math>(H,B)</math> is called a Hausdorff pre-Hilbert space.{{sfn | Trèves | 2006 | pp=112–123}}  
If <math>B</math> is non-negative then it induces a canonical [[seminorm]] on <math>H</math>, denoted by <math>\| \cdot \|</math>, defined by <math>x\mapsto B(x,x)^{1/2}</math>, where if <math>B</math> is also positive definite then this map is a [[Norm (mathematics)|norm]].{{sfn | Trèves | 2006 | pp=112–123}}  
This canonical semi-norm makes every pre-Hilbert space into a [[seminormed space]] and every Hausdorff pre-Hilbert space into a [[normed space]]. 
The sesquilinear form <math>B:H\times H\to\mathbb{C}</math> is separately uniformly continuous in each of its two arguments and hence can be extended to a separately continuous sesquilinear form on the [[Complete topological vector space|completion]] of <math>H</math>; if <math>H</math> is [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]] then this completion is a [[Hilbert space]].{{sfn | Trèves | 2006 | pp=112–123}} 
A Hausdorff pre-Hilbert space that is [[Complete space|complete]] is called a [[Hilbert space]].

=== Canonical map into the anti-dual ===

Suppose <math>(H,B)</math>is a pre-Hilbert space. If <math>h\in H</math>, we define the canonical maps:
{{bi|left=1.6|<math>B(h,\cdot):H\mapsto\mathbb{C}</math> where <math>y\mapsto B(h,y)</math>, and}}
{{bi|left=1.6|<math>B(\cdot,h):H\mapsto\mathbb{C}</math> where <math>x\mapsto B(x,y)</math>.}}
The ''canonical map''{{sfn | Trèves | 2006 | pp=112–123}}  from <math>H</math> into its anti-dual <math>\overline{H}^{\prime}</math> is the map 
{{bi|left=1.6|<math>H \to \overline{H}^{\prime}</math> defined by 
<math>x\mapsto B(x,\cdot)</math>.}}

If <math>(H,B)</math> is a pre-Hilbert space then this canonical map is linear and continuous; 
this map is an [[isometry]] onto a vector subspace of the anti-dual if and only if <math>(H,B)</math> is a Hausdorff pre-Hilbert.{{sfn | Trèves | 2006 | pp=112–123}} 

There is of course a canonical antilinear surjective isometry <math>H^{\prime} \to \overline{H}^{\prime}</math> that sends a continuous linear functional <math>f</math> on <math>H</math> to the continuous antilinear functional denoted by <math>\bar f</math> and defined by <math>x\mapsto\overline{f(x)}</math>.

== Fundamental theorem ==
{{math theorem|name=Fundamental theorem of Hilbert spaces{{sfn | Trèves | 2006 | pp=112–123}}|1=  Suppose that <math>(H,B)</math> is a [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]] [[pre-Hilbert space]] where <math>B:H\times H\to\mathbb{C}</math> is a [[sesquilinear form]] that is [[linear]] in its first coordinate and antilinear in its second coordinate. Then the canonical linear mapping from <math>H</math> into the [[anti-dual space]] of <math>H</math> is [[surjective]] if and only if <math>(H,B)</math> is a Hilbert space, in which case the canonical map is a surjective [[isometry]] of <math>H</math> onto its anti-dual.}}
